speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
maintopic: PROPOSED TARIFF PREFERENCES FOR EXPORTS FROM DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my capacity as Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs I wish to advise the House that there is a growing realization that to bridge the gap that separates the rich and poor countries the export earnings of the latter must increase substantially. One of the means that could facilitate achieving this objective is to provide the exports of these countries preferential access to world markets. I wish to inform this House of recent progress that has been made toward the elaboration of a scheme of tariff preferences that could achieve this purpose.
At the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development in New Delhi last year there was unanimous agreement to attempt to establish a system of special tariff reductions that the industrialized countries would offer the developing countries. Since then, we have been approaching the proposed system in two stages, initially, discussion within the OECD among prospective donor countries and, subsequently, discussion within UNCTAD between prospective donors and beneficiaries. We are about to move to the second stage.
The Secretary General of the OECD is today transmitting to the Secretary General of UNCTAD a report which summarizes the results of the extensive meetings that prospective donor countries have held during the past year. Attached to this report are the
818	COMMONS
Proposed Tariffs for Exports provisional proposals that the various governments which are prepared to consider extending preferences, that is, all developed countries of western Europe, North America, Australia, New Zealand and Japan, exchanged within the OECD in order to indicate the nature of the tariff preferences they were prepared to consider granting to developing countries.
Although the Canadian proposal that is being transmitted to UNCTAD, along with those of other donors, is no more than indicative hon. members will wish to be aware of its substance. In essence we have told our partners within the OECD, and now within the UNCTAD, that we are prepared to consider reducing the Canadian tariff on imports from developing countries of most manufactured and semi-manufactured goods either by one-third off the post-Kennedy round mostfavoured-nation rate, or to the level of the present British preferential rate, whichever is lower. In addition, we would consider certain tariff reductions for imports from developing countries of a selected list of agricultural products that are of particular interest to developing countries. We envisage extending these preferential rates to imports from those developing countries that are entitled to MFN or British preferential treatment.
In order to assure that the scheme will not be disruptive to the Canadian economy, we have made it clear that we would not extend these reduced rates to products which we judge to be sensitive and for which we have negotiated or are asking for a quantitative restraint on exports to Canada from any country. Moreover, we, like other prospective donors, would insist on a safeguards procedure which would permit donors to alter at any time the nature of the preferences they are offering, to withhold the grant of a preference from the beginning or to withdraw a preferential rate which had been in effect.
We are confident that our indicative proposal contains the elements which will provide substantial new opportunities for developing country exporters. We would assure developing countries a preference of at least one-third off the MFN rate. However, since the present British preferential rate is in many instances less than two-thirds of the MFN rate, for those items we would be offering a preference considerably in excess of one-third of the MFN rate. In fact, for an extensive number of items we would be offering to remove the duty entirely on imports from developing countries. It will be realized

DEBATES	November 14, 1969
that our purpose in offering to harmonize the proposed new preferences with our present British preferential rate is to equalize the treatment accorded by Canada to exports from all developing countries.
There is a great variety in the various indicative proposals of our OECD partners. Some of our OECD partners have said they are willing to offer a greater tariff reduction than we are proposing. However, unlike several other donor countries the linear cut in our tariff for imports from developing countries that we are proposing is not qualified by restrictions on the quantities to be imported, nor is it our intention to exclude whole sectors of trade from the scheme.
We wish to stress that our proposal is tentative and subject to revision following further discussion abroad and in Canada. One of the basic principles of the proposed scheme, accepted by all the industrialized countries that have stated a willingness to participate in it, is that the burden will be shared equitably amongst all donors. We have not yet completed our assessment of the various indicative proposals of our OECD partners. The details of the United States and Japanese proposals only became known to us last week. It is possible that the system of tariff preferences we hope in due course to put before the House for consideration and approval will differ from that which I just outlined.
However, in spite of the tentative nature of this proposal we believed that members would wish to be aware of its substance and the state of play of the efforts to elaborate an international scheme of tariff preferences for the exports of developing countries.
When the OECD document I referred to earlier in this statement becomes available in Ottawa I would be pleased to make it available for tabling.

We take the position that we should do all we can, consistent with our obligations to our own people in Canada and to our other international commitments, to ensure that the countries to which the hon. gentleman referred do develop to a point at which they will be beyond the type of violence in evidence in developing countries in so many parts of the world, in the hope that in due course they will become Canada's partners in trade and on the international scene. Mr. Speaker, I noticed that the minister, when reading the statement, dropped the word "hypothetical", but whether that changes the nature of the statement is another matter. Everyone who has studied international aid has recognized for many years that trade is one of the most important problems that developing countries have to face. This is repeated and emphasized in the recent report of the international committee of which the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson was chairman. Therefore, without any reservation I greet not only the government statement but also the statement that work is progressing on the part of the
DEBATES	819
Proposed Tariffs for Exports Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development to deal with this problem in some effective way.
I have but three comments to make. It is characteristic of the relationship between the developed and the developing countries and of the paternalistic attitude that we in the developed countries take that in all of the discussions that are taking place it is the developed countries that decide what they are going to present to the poor developing countries. We take unto ourselves the right unilaterally to withdraw, to withhold or to change any tariff arrangements that are made, and in all of these discussions the developing countries are treated like mendicants sitting at our feet as we hand out some largesse. This approach is evident throughout the statement that the minister made, and I object in the strongest possible language to this attitude that is taken by the rich countries of the world.
The developing countries have a right to participate in these discussions, to discuss with the donor countries what they would like to have done and to have some influence on the decisions that the donor countries make, instead of this club of the rich deciding what the poor are going to get, with the poor people given no opportunity to participate. It is particularly reprehensible to me that this attitude should come from a government that talks so much about participatory democracy at home. I suggest the same holds true on the international plan as it does within any one of our societies.
My second point is that not only are tariff reductions and preferential tariffs important to trade with the developing countries but equally important are the prices of some of the primary products that these countries may be able to export. The fact is that the rich countries of the world have taken the usual selfish advantage of the market situation and have depressed the price of many of these primary products to the level where their export would not do the developing countries much good.
Finally, I urge the minister that the House be given more information when he or the Secretary of State for External Affairs next makes a statement on this subject. I ask that we be told what products are being discussed, the countries that are involved and what general range of tariff reductions is being considered so that, instead of a general blurb such as the minister was handed by some officer to

Mr. Speaker, before I speak on the subject with which the minister dealt this morning, I would like to draw his attention to the most important fact that, in the opinion of the government, our federal institutions must be bilingual. I thank the minister for having relayed to me the text of his statement, but it was in English, and I would rather have had it in French. At any rate, I think that the departments should make sure that we are forwarded the French and English texts of the statements made by the ministers.
To come back to the matter discussed by the minister, namely the aid that developed countries can give to developing countries, I would like to recall some of the things he said in his statement, and I quote:

-we are prepared to consider reducing the Canadian tariff on imports from developing countries of most manufactured and semi-manufactured goods either by one-third off the post-Kennedy round ... or to the level of the present British preferential rate-

And later on, he said that we will import from developing countries.

-a selected list of agricultural products that are of particular interest to developing countries.

Of course, we support the government when it decides to help developing countries. But the minister should consider the situation and realize that, at the very moment when we are preparing to help developing countries, the government adopts legislation aimed at curtailing domestic assistance as much as possible, and this is a paradox.
In fact, we could help those countries while ensuring the normal growth of our own economy. For instance, we should examine the factors which prompt us to cut down our economic activities while we help developing countries by importing their products. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said earlier that the rich decide what the poor have to take, to accept from us, that the decision rests with us, all of which is not so very democratic, etc.

DEBATES	November 14, 1969
There I disagree with the hon. member for York South because it is clear that the prices of agricultural products and manufactured and semi-manifactured goods we import from those countries are much lower than those prevailing here in Canada. If we import them duty-free, we will be competing with our own economy, which is not logical.
I believe that in the circumstances it is not a matter of deciding what products developing countries should be forced to take from us. As a matter of fact, as the minister himself has said, we are ready to import goods from those countries if this is likely to help them. Nevertheless, I maintain my point, that in so doing we should beware of hampering our own economic development and we must see to improving our production and bringing our costs down through increased production.
We should not neglect our own economy while devising a foreign policy that would bring about unemployment and would confront our producers with rather unfair competition.
I suggest we should wait for the minister to draw up a list of farm products and manufactured or semi-manufactured goods to be purchased from those countries.
In any case, the statement holds that assistance should be extended to developing countries, and we agree to that as long as it is not at the expense of our own economic development.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have to day before us another railway bill. This has become somewhat routine in the last few years since a similar bill has been introduced every session.
In fact, for several years now, the Canadian National Railways have been facing the same problems and every year, the government introduces almost similar bills which do not bring any answer to the problems facing this Crown Corporation.
Recently the CNR and the CPR have made representations in order to be granted permission to abandon a number of passenger services. The people of my area which I represent are particularly concerned with this application.
Among the services to be abandoned are those of the Abitibi and Lake St. John regions which are serviced by the CNR.
Among the other services which would fall victim to this measure are those between Montreal and Vancouver.
The justification for such applications lies in the losses incurred which are due to the fact that passengers are gradually discarding that means of transportation.
When we start considering how the CNR is run, we discover that there are far too many officials in this company and too few executives.
I have here before me an application which was made two or three years ago by agencies operating in the small northwestern town of Quebec where I live, I mean La Sarre. This application was made in the light of the fact that some other towns in this area such as Amos, Rouyn-Noranda, Val d'Or, Malartic and Senneterre enjoy free parcel delivery service, provided by the CNR, while La Sarre is
November 14. 1969	COMMONS
excluded. The people of La Sarre were entitled to the same service provided in other communities, since this is a profitable service.
Therefore, I made representations to the CNR in order to get the same service for La Sarre. Here is the answer I received in a letter from Quebec, dated April 16, 1968 and signed by Mr. L. M. Poitevin, director of the Quebec area. I quote:
In our answer dated September 26, 1967, we pointed out that according to a check of the volume of small shipments, there had been a fairly substantial decrease compared to the 1965 volume and also a decrease in comparison with 1966. We also said we wished to see the effect that the new rates coming into force at the beginning of September 1957 would have on volume. We added that a fairly substantial increase in shipments in La Sarre would be desirable in order to prove that the collecting and distributing service free of charge, but which would entail great expenditures, would still be profitable.
The ridiculous side of it all is that the CNR insist upon the patrons being sufficient in number before granting them services, while in private enterprise, it is quite the opposite. Good service is provided to people so that they will become customers.
While private enterprise gets good results through this method, public enterprise will not use it. It would like to be sure to have customers before offering them services. It is not surprising that the Canadian public, as much in Abitibi as elsewhere, should shun the services of the CNR which is thus pursuing a cheese-paring policy.
We find again the same situation in the passenger service on the line to Abitibi. To save money, the Montreal-Abitibi and Mont-real-Lac Saint-Jean services have been merged through a transfer point at Hervey-Jonction. Then, there is complete disregard for the people who want to go to Abitibi or to the Lac Saint-Jean and come back.
And when the travelling public uses other means of transportation the company claims a deficit or a lack of users to abandon the service.
I think that any petition aimed at abandoning a service is really an application for subsidies. I ask the government to consider carefully the CNR application.
The annual report of the CNR for 1968 is full of interesting comments and figures.
In Bill C-7, the minister asks for the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the CNR system in Canada and Air Canada.
DEBATES	831
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada
If the CN shows a deficit in some of its services, would it not be appropriate to investigate a little its financing methods?
The report emphasizes the fact that the operating revenues-rail operations, hotels and telecommunications operations and so on for the year 1968-showed a surplus of $41.2 million but because of the way it is run the CN had to pay $70.4 million in interest for that same year which turned a $41 million surplus into a $29.2 million deficit.
When we, of the Ralliement creditiste, ask as we have been doing for a long time, that publicly-owned companies at the federal, provincial and municipal levels, be financed interest-free by the Bank of Canada, some government members find our contention ridiculous.
However, such an approach would make it possible for the Crown corporations to show operating surpluses, instead of constantly operating in the red as they do now, because of the orthodox way in which the government finances its own Crown corporations.
We know that when the government bought the bonds of the CNR-its own company-it did so with borrowed money. The CNR pays 4 per cent interest on the bonds bought by the government of Canada. The revenue from the recent sale of bonds-the amount mentioned in the bill is $82 million-will be used to redeem bonds that have reached maturity. What are we to think then of the publicity in the newspapers and over the radio-which costs thousands of dollars-according to which the government is offering the "best ever" bonds? Those bonds bear an interest of 8J. Money is borrowed from the public to grant a loan of $82 million to the C.N.R., at 4 per cent interest. Talk about a deal!
This is standard management practice: no wonder the government is always in the red.
On the last page of the CNR report, there is a complete list of statistics for the last 25 years which indicate that the CNR had profits for 6 years and losses for 19 due to the interest payments. Over the last 25 year-period, the CNR paid $1,240,990,000 in interest on its debt.
Mr. Speaker, we know that interest, through the federal government, was channelled back, not to the government, but to those who lend money to the government, which in turn lends it to the CNR.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that that procedure is not only ridiculous but criminal. Some find the Creditistes proposals ridiculous, but I claim that this orthodox way of financing public
November 14, 1969
832	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada services is criminal, because money is taken from the individuals and given to the various loan companies.
If the government financed the expenditures of the Canadian National Railways, Air Canada and the St. Lawrence Seaway-all three are in the same situation-through interest-free loans from the Bank of Canada, it would be possible to reduce passenger or freight rates or increase the wages of the employees of those companies. Thus, everyone would be satisfied, which is not the case today.
One provision of Bill C-7 provides for a sum of $19 million to be used for the construction of branch lines by the CNR Therefore, I would ask the Minister without portfolio who sponsors the bill, where the CNR intends to build branch lines.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I have been told that the CNR intends to build a branch line from Matagami to James Bay. I would like to ask the minister whether it is true and when the construction of that branch line is anticipated?
This is why I say that the bill should be referred to the committee, in order to be thoroughly studied.
The management of the Crown Corporations is not satisfactory and should be improved. I ask the government to take as soon as possible the necessary measures and not to introduce such bills every year-since that does not solve the problems of Crown Corporations-but a legislation to enable the Crown Corporations to serve the public in the best interests of the nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must avail myself of this opportunity today to refer briefly to railway companies, and especially to the CN in the Sague-nay-Lac-Saint-Jean region.
I know that this bill deals with the annual financing of CN operations and that it is not necessarily the right time to discuss all the policies of this company.
As it was announced recently that passenger services were to be dropped in our region and in other parts of Canada, I must add my voice to that of my hon. friend, the member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise), since both our regions have already been affected by a recent decision of the CN.
The region of Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean, with its population of some 300,000 inhabitants, has only one railway service. In our
[Mr. Laprise.l

region, there is no competition between the CN and the CP. The CN cannot therefore claim that competition prevented it from making any profit in the past.
If now the CN sees fit to reduce its passenger service because it is no longer patronized to the same extent as before, it is the first to blame, because in the past 15 years, the service has been getting worse all the time.
At present, to travel from the Saguenay region to Montreal, a distance of 300 miles, one has to spend more than 12 hours in CN trains.
How can you expect the public to support such a service? In short, if there is any competition in the area, it is within the CN. The company is striving by every means to make its service as unattractive as possible, as though some genius in their administration were trying to plan the service in such a way that people will give it up as soon as possible.
Let us, for instance, look at the sleeping-car service. The train only has one sleeping-car. Can it be used? Hardly, because during the past three years, the price of single roomettes has increased from $5 to $10, a double roomette now costs $20', just to spend a few hours in a bed. Moreover passengers are jostled from side to side which makes it difficult to sleep, because the line is in such a poor condition. How then can the public be expected to make use of the CN passenger service?
Mr. Speaker, my area is served by Quebec-air and Air Canada. There are also bus services and we have good roads, but nevertheless, some people still travel by train and will do so as long as possible.
If this company treated its customers better, I am sure things would turn out differently. As a matter of fact, the experience has already been made. A few years ago, a Mr. Delagrave had been appointed vice president in charge of CN passenger service. He had taken it upon himself to increase the number of passengers travelling on the CN, and he actually achieved his goal. But in view of this man's achievement, the authorities make life impossible for him in order to force him to seek employment elsewhere. So he left the CN and now works for another company, because he realized that his policy was totally at variance with that of CN authorities who obviously wanted to do away with the passenger service.
We can only oppose the policy of the Canadian National Railways designed to curtail the passenger service. I do not object to
November 14, 1969

my hon. friend from Abitibi or any citizen of that part of western Quebec travelling aboard the train I am on, because I believe that is how one meets very interesting people. I am sure that the merger of services in our two areas is quite possible. However, I do not think it was necessary to lengthen the trip by an hour and a half, as is the case since both services were merged.
As far as the Lac-Saint-Jean people are concerned, we have to wait an hour and a half on the train. Such an arrangement simply indicates poor planning of the time table for the trains from Abitibi. There are no reasons for both trains, the Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean line and the Abitibi line, not to arrive at the same time at Hervey-Jonction. It is a simple question of planning, but they have made it so that they shall not meet, in order that one or the other be forced to wait for an hour and a half.
In view of this, I personally object to the Canadian National Railways being granted the right to reduce or completely discontinue its services in the Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean region and the Abitibi region as well.
I object to that for many reasons. Both our regions are designated areas under the government policy. They need additional assistance. If I understand the assistance policy scheme to designated areas, assistance is needed in the establishment of a substructure, in order that these regions may prove more attractive to industries interested in settling there.
Now, it is certainly not by reducing the services that exist now or by simply eliminating them as the Canadian National Railways intends to do that we are going to improve the substructure in the Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean and Abitibi regions which are designated areas, parts of which will be considered special. Then, why reduce service while other departments are trying through millions of dollars in subsidies to improve the situation and raise the employment level in these regions?
In addition to the passenger service, there is in the Saguenay, a transportation service for first class goods which must be delivered quickly. The elimination of this service will deprive certain enterprises in our region of these goods. They will have to find other ways of getting them at, of course, a higher cost.
I do not intend to delay further second reading of this bill so that it may be referred

Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada to the Committee on Transport and Communications, but I join those who spoke before me in asking the government to pay close attention to the proceedings of the Canadian Transportation Commission to avoid that at this level of administration a unilateral decision be made, which would deprive Canadians of the services they are entitled to.

Mr. Speaker, it is almost one year ago that the last measure similar in nature and design to Bill C-7 was before the House. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) remarked last night, this bill rarely changes in form or concept. It is what could be termed an annual bill, a perfunctory measure which unfortunately in too many cases has received automatic and often swift passage through the House.
However, that does not apply this year-at least, I hope not. If my few words delay its passage a little, then I will feel I have succeeded; and I shall proceed to tell the House why I would not want the bill to go through without my having made some observations about it.
We had considerable discussion on this measure last year because at that time the people of my province were confronted with an accomplished fact, namely the abandonment by the Canadian National Railways of its rail passenger services in that province. I well recall saying at the time-my colleagues voiced similar sentiments-that there but for the grace of God go other provinces. Today, we see that other provinces are indeed going to lose all, or certainly part, of their railway passenger services. In this connection, I need only refer to the comments of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the very impressive remarks of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), e (12:40 p.m.)
When the legislation goes to the committee, Mr. Speaker, I hope the members of the committee will exercise the right that is theirs to examine the reasons for the decisions that have been made, and to exercise that control over the operations of railways in this country, especially the operations of the Canadian National Railways, that should be ours but which in actual fact is not. During the Committee hearings I intend to press for those reasons underlying the applications now before the Canadian Transport Commission to abandon rail passenger service in certain
November 14, 1969
834	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada parts of the country. We are especially interested in my part of the country because we were the reluctant guinea pigs. They tried out this idea on us first. Perhaps the House might be interested in knowing what the position is in Newfoundland at the present time.
In accordance with the directives of the Canadian Transport Commission, the rolling stock of our rail passenger service is being held in reserve, supposedly to meet an emergency or to cope with adverse conditions brought on by weather or some other act of God which the bus services cannot handle. It is rather interesting that the old "Bullet" is not dead yet. During the recent Liberal leadership convention in Newfoundland, the Liberal party, which did so little to prevent this injustice to my province, suddenly discovered that the old "Bullet" still had one more useful function to perform. They dusted off the Pullman cars, took the boards off the windows, and used them to accommodate 200 or 300 delegates to that convention.
The premier himself, acting like the proletarian he likes to think he is, insisted that he should have an upper berth. I bet it is the first time he has had the privilege of sleeping in an upper berth, albeit a stationary one. Those who slept on the "Bullet" during the convention were boasting that they had slept on the "Bullet" with Joey. That is what became of our rail passenger service. It is being held in reserve for an act of God, and certainly the Liberal leadership convention should qualify. It could only be by Divine Providence that the Liberal party in Newfoundland finds itself in the mess it is today.
There are other aspects of the service about which we are concerned. We are concerned, for example, about the operation of the buses in Newfoundland. We want to be reassured that the bus service will be able to cope with weather conditions. We should like to know what complaints the railway is receiving from people who have to use this service. We want to know what their plans are to improve the service. We should like also to know what the intentions are regarding the coastal service in Newfoundland.
In my province, the CNR has the responsibility of providing mail and passenger service around the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador which is inaccessible by road or other modes of transportation. There are ominous signs that the railway company would like to discontinue this service as well; in fact, the wheels have already been set in motion. Two of the ships that were providing 

this service to the constituency represented by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) have been sold, with the result that today the people using the service, the only means by which one can travel along that south coast of Newfoundland, have to be piled in like cattle. There is no berth accommodation and there is no seating accommodation. Last summer I saw women and children literally sitting on the floor because the two vessels now are inadequate. The railway company knows this, as does the Minister of Transport and the Canadian Transport Commission, yet nobody seems inclined to do anything about it. I serve notice on the CNR that I want answers to some of these questions.
I should like to know what the future is, if any, of the East Coast ferry service which was provided in accordance with the terms of union. It is now operating between eastern Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. There have been suggestions, indeed charges have been made, that this service is purposely being downgraded by the railway company. This complaint does not relate to the services offered, because this vessel provides excellent services. The service is being downgraded in respect of promotion and advertising. It seems to be the best kept secret in this country that there is a 10,000 ton vessel operating between Argentia, Newfoundland and Sydney, Nova Scotia, and that this vessel does in fact save at least 500 miles of driving. There is no evidence that this excellent service is promoted and there is no evidence of advertising. There have actually been cases of people applying in Sydney for passage over to Newfoundland who have been told the only way to get there was by crossing over from Sydney to Port-Aux-Basques and that there was no way of avoiding the long drive across Newfoundland. We should like to know why the railway company is not promoting or advertising this service.
More particularly, we should like to know why the rates are so high for this service. It costs $50 to put your car on this boat. By the time you pay for your own ticket, berth accommodation and meals it costs you about $100. Who can afford to use this service which is provided for tourists? No tourist is going to spend $100 when he knows he can save perhaps $50 by taking that long drive across Newfoundland. The railway company has made no move toward reducing the rates. I maintain the rates should be reduced by at least 25 per cent. There is very strong evidence that the company intends to remove this vessel from this service and place it in
November 14, 1969	COMMONS DEBATES
service elsewhere. We should like to know why this service is not promoted and why the railway company has not accepted recommendations from many people and organizations such as boards of trade, members of parliament and the travelling public to reduce the rates. A 25 per cent reduction would certainly have the effect of increasing the traffic and consequently would offset any loss of revenue. We want to know what the future of this service is and we want to be assured that this undertaking by the government of Canada, cemented as it is in the terms of union, will be carried out.
There is another matter of tremendous importance to Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces. It is so important and has such a tremendous effect on the cost of living and the inflationary trend that I am surprised it has not been alluded to by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Bas-ford). I refer to the lifting of the freeze on freight rates in the Atlantic provinces, in eastern Quebec or that area covered by the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I refer also to the consequential 11 per cent increase in rates announced the day after the freeze was lifted. Perhaps the record should note that this lifting of the freeze and the consequential increase in rates by the railway company-in other words this action on the part of the government-was contrary to the recommendations of the Atlantic premiers, contrary to the recommendations of the Maritime Transportation Commission, and contrary to the recommendations of boards of trade, shippers and almost everyone in the Atlantic provinces.
What did the Atlantic premiers have to say about this action in a statement released by the four premiers of the Atlantic provinces in March of this year? On page 23 of their statement, we read this:

The reasons for the establishment of the freeze in the first instance are just as valid today as when the National Transportation Act was passed by Parliament. The Atlantic Provinces recommend, therefore, that the Federal Government take the necessary steps either by legislation or by agreement to maintain the freeze on Atlantic Provinces rail rates until such time as the new regional transportation policy is effected.
Of course, they are referring to the long awaited, many times promised, new policy on Atlantic transportation. That is what the four premiers recommended just a few months ago, yet the decision of the government, effective in September, was completely contrary to their recommendations. How did the premiers
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada react when they learned that their recommendations to the federal government were totally and completely disregarded by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), and by his colleagues in the federal government? Their reaction was one of dismay, incredulity and shock. I shall quote now from the Globe and Mail of September 26:
Premiers protest rate freeze
The Atlantic Premiers Conference meeting here yesterday termed the federal government's decision to lift the Atlantic Provinces freight rate freeze as being "in conflict with the underlying philosophy of the federal Government's announced policy toward the alleviation of regional disparity."
A strongly worded statement released at the end of the day-long meeting said the conference "vigorously protests the unilateral decision," which was made "without prior consultation with the governments of the Atlantic Provinces."
The story goes on to say that the premiers, to put it mildly, were surprised. They saw this action for what it was and were not hesitant in saying that this was a unilateral decision, without consultation with the Atlantic provinces, notwithstanding the fact that this government, the Minister of Transport and the other ministers from the Atlantic provinces knew full well the effect that a lifting of the freeze would have. They knew it would have a consequential effect in the form of a boost in the rates charged by the railways. These freight rate increases contribute greatly to the increased cost of living and the inflation which is already taking such a toll on the people who live in the regionally depressed areas of this country. What does the Evening Telegram say about it? In an editorial dated September 23 it termed this decision as a last straw. The lead editorial had this to say:
Just in case things weren't bad enough in Newfoundland's cost of living another jolt is on the way. The freight rate for goods moving to this province is to be increased by 11 per cent beginning today.
Now we are told the freeze was lifted and the railways were permitted to increase the rates because the subsidies under the MFRA would be applied to the trucking industry under the new legislation. That is fine except for the fact-and the Minister of Transport knows this better than anyone-that there is no trucking into Newfoundland because the truckers cannot afford to pay the exorbitant freight rates across the gulf or on the east coast ferry, rates which were set to prevent the trucking industry from providing competition for the railways. So, there is no truck transportation of any consequence going into Newfoundland such as in the other three

Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada maritime provinces. Therefore, when the Minister of Transport tells the truckers to cut their freight rates, this has no meaning at all for us. It makes no difference whether they reduce their rates or increase them; we are still dependent to a very large extent on rail transportation.
In speaking of the trucking industry, my colleague the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) referred earlier today to the recently announced increase in trucking rates right across the country. This is the answer to the Minister of Transport from the trucking industry in the Atlantic provinces. He tells them the freeze has been taken off so that the railways will be happy. The railways are happy because the freeze is lifted and they are permitted to raise their rates. Today, their rates are 11 per cent higher than they were before the freeze took place.
Every report I can find, and all the editorials by senior editors who have commented on this situation, contain the same opinion. Perhaps this opinion can best be summed up by reading a brief quotation from the Saint John Daily News of September 26:
All this must be intimately related to the problem ot regional economic disparity.
We have enough problems already in the Atlantic provinces. We also suffer the consequences of our geographical and regional disparity. These include the high cost of living, the excessively high unemployment and the continuing problem of excessively high freight rates. Now, we look to the government for some succour, for some relief. We look to the Minister of Transport who presents himself as the great spokesman for the Atlantic provinces. We look to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) and all the ministers from the Atlantic provinces. We look to the Minister without Portfolio and we look to the Prime Minister and his just society for some relief.


What do we get? We get a unilateral decision made by this government without consultation with either the Atlantic provinces, the Maritime Transportation Commission or anybody. They unilaterally break faith with the people of the Atlantic provinces by announcing a lifting of the freeze and by permitting the railways to increase their rates by 11 per cent, thereby adding to the already unbearable burden the people of the Atlantic provinces must carry because of the consequences of excessively high transportation rates.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment for lunch I was outlining to the House the disastrous effects on the economy and on the people of the Atlantic provinces of the government's decision to lift the freeze on freight rates and the consequential 11 per cent increase in the freight rates by the railways. During my remarks I referred to the brief entitled "The Basic Elements of an Atlantic Provinces Transportation Policy" which was presented in March to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) by the four premiers of the Atlantic provinces, in which certain specific recommendations were made to which the government arbitrarily refused to adhere. I referred to the government's attitude toward this brief and the reaction of the four premiers following the lifting of the freeze and the increase in the rates.

Feelings in the Atlantic provinces on this matter are unanimous. Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada
The freeze has been lifted and the rates have been increased. Since Mr. Pickersgill became Chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission, Newfoundland has lost its rail passenger service and is losing its coastal service. The maritime provinces are going to lose their rail passenger service into St. John's if the CPR has its way. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this legislation for the financing of the Canadian National immediately raises the question of a railway company's behaviour and how that squares with its obligation to the public. The implications of the recent request by both of Canada's major railways for wholesale abandonment of passenger service across the country are of tremendous
November 14, 1969
840	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada national importance. They expose the very core of one of the greatest challenges our modern society faces, the challenge of providing transportation that is swift, economical and adequate.
At this time, I am more interested in the implications for the province of Manitoba arising from specific requests for abandonment of passenger services by both railroads-requests which, if granted, could deal a heavy social and economic blow to central and northern Manitoba. We have the Canadian Pacific Railway's request to abandon all passenger service, including the transcontinental service. Winnipeg is a vital point on the route. I am more particularly concerned about the Canadian National's request to suspend passenger service on the Winnipeg-Dau-phin-The Pas-Gillam-Churchill run and on the Wabowden-Gillam-Churchill line. I agree that it is unfair and unrealistic for us to compel a system such as the Canadian National to operate at a deficit of more than $3 million a year, which is the loss claimed on the Winnipeg-Churchill service. The Canadian National, after all, is a publicly owned system that came into existence in the public interest after an amalgamation of a group of bankrupt railway companies. It is true that it has been a charge on the public purse ever since, and has received assistance from the public purse.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
But the Canadian National Railway is in a very different position from the privately owned Canadian Pacific Railway which received many great concessions from the people of Canada that enabled it to make tremendous profits over the years in lines of endeavour other than railway passenger service. For this reason, I believe the two groups of applications must be considered entirely separate. In my opinion, the CNR is using its applications to abandon passenger service on 13 runs across the country more as a signal for help than with the serious intent of dropping service.
The CPR, on the other hand, obviously wants out of the whole passenger carrying chore because it is no longer profitable. This railway wants the public that gave it the concessions which led to tremendous corporate development and handsome profits over the years to now allow it to get out of the obligations that were the reason for the concessions in the first place. These concessions included $25 million in cash before the turn of the century, plus 25 million acres of


land. It was these concessions, given in return for a transcontinental rail line, that permitted the CPR to build hotels, get into land deals, mining and smelting and airlines, not to mention the very lucrative freight haulage business.
There is an excellent editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune of November 11 that deals with specific concessions given the CPR by Manitoba and the city of Winnipeg. In the matter of real property taxes, the CPR was given a perpetual exemption. Lawyers and management for the CPR have always argued that this original bargain should be kept. They are meticulous in making what payments they choose to make as an act of grace, not as a legal obligation. The CPR part of the bargain that led to these generous tax concessions was to supply rail service. What is sauce of the goose must be sauce for the gander. If the CPR expects the Canadian people and their various governments to abide strictly by the original bargain, then surely the CPR should be willing to abide by it.
Both railways have over the years been subsidized for losses incurred in supplying what are deemed to be necessary public services. This system is in the process of change, but the principle is still recognized and will be continued. In the light of this principle and the original bargain struck, I think the barefaced proposal of the CPR to pull out of all passenger service is farcical and insulting.
To return to my immediate concern which is Manitoba, and particularly the social and economic life of central and northern Manitoba, I believe the CNR should not be allowed to simply drop all passenger service to places such as Thompson, The Pas and Churchill, not to mention Dauphin and other centres. Although advances have been made in bus and air travel, the fact remains that there are many people who still prefer rail travel or, indeed, cannot use any other mode. They may not exist in sufficient numbers to make the service economically sound, but that is not a valid excuse for dropping that service. It is a necessary public service and should be regarded as such. If money is needed to sustain it, this should be forthcoming from the public purse. I have often suspected that to strengthen the economic argument the railways, the CPR at least, have deliberately discouraged passengers through poor and awkward service. This sort of thing is really not good enough when we consider the vital
November 14, 1969

importance of transportation to national development and to meeting some of the tremendous problems of our modern urbanized and far-flung society.
In my opinion, the Canadian Transport Commission cannot possibly consent to these applications in their present form and still pretend to be protecting the public interest. I would rather see the CTC admit that there is little likelihood of necessary passenger service ever being economically profitable and start examining the problem, not negatively by allowing cancellations, but positively by looking for ways to make them economically sound. If both railways realized that they were in the passenger carrying business to stay, they might assist in positive research.
I have in mind such things as pioneering more modern, smaller passenger units. This has been done to a limited extent in the Toronto and Montreal areas where commuter business is the only paying passenger business the railways have. There are the Montreal commuter runs, the Rapido between Toronto and Montreal and the provincial government's commuter trains in and around metro Toronto. Something of this spirit should be carried into provincial, interprovincial and transcontinental travel.
In Britain, the government and British Railways are spending some $30 million in developing a high-speed, modern passenger train. When we consider that it takes an estimated $20 million to develop a new automobile and approximately $32 million to build a mile or so of elevated expressway, surely this amount of money spent on development and use of existing rail lines might well be a better investment of public money. We are going to have to transport more and more people every year, not fewer. We are going to have to pour more and more public money into providing assistance to provinces and communities to help to meet this problem of passenger transportation. It might be wise to look at what facilities already exist and what use may be made of them by adaption and improvement before we pour out money to construct new facilities that too often only add to the tangle, and complicate and aggravate the problem.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like simply to make the strongest protest, first, against the blanket proposal of the CPR to abandon all passenger service and, second, against the application of the CNR to isolate central and northern Manitoba from the mainstream of provincial and national life by dropping passenger service on the Winnipeg-
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada Churchill line and its subsidiaries. Financing the CNR is an annual necessity, but it should be done with a clear restatement of the company's obligation to the Canadian public.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to make a few comments on the bill before us. Before doing so, I wish to endorse the comments made generally by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Thomson) when he was talking about the Canadian Pacific Railway.
At the outset, I wish to say I am quite disturbed by the recent activities of the CPR in attempting to drop as much passenger service as possible. We must look back to 1881 when the Canadian Pacific Railway Act was passed in this House. In that Act, we find many of the concessions that were given to the company at that time. Among these concessions were $25 million in money, which I remind hon. members was worth much more then than now. They were given a huge parcel of land and certain mineral concessions as well. In return for these, Canadian Pacific promised the people of Canada they would provide passenger service on an everlasting basis. We must ensure that this company continues to keep that promise to the people of Canada.
I am somewhat disturbed by recent indications that the Canadian National Railways wants to abandon some of its passenger services as well. The citizens all across Canada will need these services for many years to come.
The bill before us is similar to bills which have been presented to this House for many years to finance the operations of Canadian National Railways and Air Canada. Instead of just presenting this bill every year, Mr. Speaker, I would like to hear the government talk about transportation policy, a policy which needs to be changed and needs to be flexible in our vast and ever-changing world.
There is one difference in the bill presented this year. If I understand correctly, the CNR is no longer handling money for Air Canada. I ask the minister, when he makes his remarks later this afternoon, to clarify this point. What does this actually mean? Why is the CNR no longer the middle man for Air Canada? Does this mean that Air Canada is going to be moving more and more toward decreasing public control of its operations? We have noticed suggestions to this effect in the press already.
November 14, 1969

Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada
I wish to quote from an article which appeared in the Financial Post of November 1, 1969. The headline reads, "Air Canada Wants to Win Confidence of Investors". I quote:
The exact shape of Air Canada's corporate financial future remains to be thrashed out between the airline and the government.
But in the meantime, as Air Canada's chairman and chief executive officer Yves Pratt puts it, Canada's largest airline is moving steadily toward becoming more profit-oriented.
The target is to get the company's earning picture up to the point where investors and lending institutions would consider it an attractive investment proposition. And that, it is generally held, means a return on investment of perhaps 10 per cent. Last year, a good one for Air Canada with a profit of $8.2 million turned up a return of 6.3 per cent.
e (2:40 p.m.)
When the minister replies I should like him to clarify this portion of the bill, because I think it is most important. The railways talk about getting out of their obligation to provide passenger service, and one of the reasons they give is that it is a losing proposition. Air Canada is making a profit. Let us make sure it continues to be publicly owned and that it is not sold to private interests.
At this point, I should like to quote from another article which I believe helps to emphasize the point I am trying to make. This is taken from the Gazette, of April 2, 1969, and the headline reads: "Air Canada Doubles Profit, Raises Rate of Return."
Air Canada had a net income of $8,184,000 in 1968, the sixth year in which it has shown a profit and double that reported in 1967, Transport Minister Paul Hellyer announced Tuesday.
The Crown-owned airline will need more than $300,000,000 in outside financing, however, to buy new equipment and property in the next five years, it was stated in the company's report tabled by Mr. Hellyer in the Commons.
The 1968 profit was the 15th for the airline in the last 18 years. It represented a return on investment of 6.3 per cent-up from 5.2 per cent the previous year.
A profit of $3,547,000 was reported during Canada's centennial year.
It is obvious that the airline is more than paying its way.
I should like to make one or two further brief comments before I close. First of all, I believe we must look at the transport situation generally and outline some of the basic objectives we wish to achieve. Above all, transportation in this country ought to be regarded as a service at all times. It must be run with social awareness and responsibility; it must be responsive to the needs of people

in whatever part of Canada they live, whether the maritimes or on the prairies or in some industrial city. In addition, the transport system must be run as cheaply as possible, and in terms not of making a profit but of providing a service to the country. It must be highly efficient, and this means schedules which allow people to move as fast and as cheaply as possible.
One might ask how it would be possible to provide such a system in this country. First, it should, in my view, be publicly owned by the people of this country because only in this way would it be possible to draft a detailed and realistic plan for transportation in Canada. In the case of a publicly owned system, we could have some say as to the manner in which it should be set up, the rates which are charged, and so on. I believe that under public ownership the operation would be more efficient. Arrangements could be made for flights to smaller communities on a more regular basis, and schedules would correspond to the needs of the people much more closely than they do at present.
I wish to say a few words, now, about regional carriers; perhaps the minister could comment on this aspect when he replies. Let me say at the outset that I should like to see the regional carriers integrated as closely as possible with Air Canada and the domestic nation wide airline already in existence. If this were done, greater service to our people would result and I hope it is the intention of the government to encourage action on these lines. Regional carriers should be approved only when it is absolutely necessary to do so; if Air Canada can fly into the areas concerned it should provide the service there.
In conclusion, let me say this: to me, it appears the government is seeking to decrease public ownership in the transportation field by using the back door, and I would ask the minister to comment on this aspect of the legislation before us when he replies.

I wish to take the opportunity offered by this debate to put on record a few remarks about transportation matters in general, though I shall address myself in particular, of course, to the bill for second reading and reference to the committee with which we are now dealing.
Last night the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) dealt very ably with the overall transportation picture. He dealt, also, with this request for increased funds for Air Canada, and I was pleased to note that he
November 14, 1969

made extensive reference to the efforts which have lately been made to make the corporation independent of the government. As we know, there is provision here for a method by which the corporation can obtain its own funds through the issuance of bonds. Many of us on this side have advocated for years, both in the House and in committee, that the company should be given an opportunity to stand on its own two feet, separate from the government, and compete with CPA and the other airlines of the world.
We believe this is a good corporation. We believe there are some disadvantages in its being tied to the government, and we hope that the measure of independence for which provision is made in these proposals will be expended further and that the day will come when Air Canada can become a separately-owned company with stock available to the public in some way.
A few months ago there was considerable talk about various reports which were to be made to the government. I recall that the present Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson) was commissioned to deal with some sort of study concerning the question of Air Canada financing and the possibility of making the company a separate entity. I hope the minister, when he replies, will tell us about these reports: are they available, and what exactly did they say about Air Canada and its future? I am referring to the report which the Minister of Supply and Services was dealing with and to another interdepartmental report involving financing-I think the committee included among its members some people from financial circles in Montreal and Toronto. It is important that we should know exactly what the government has in mind when we are being asked once again for money for Air Canada.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) dealt extensively with the subject of transportation during his speech last night. It was a good review. I do not agree with his philosophy about public ownership, but as an old Conservative I am beginning to wonder just where the Canadian Pacific Railway fits into this picture nowadays. I have said before in this House, and I say again, that it is difficult to know where the responsibility of the Canadian Pacific Railway to maintain passenger services begins and ends. According to recent information from press releases we gather that applications are being made in the proper form by both the Canadian Pacific and the

Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada Canadian National railway companies to abandon 31 passenger routes across the country. I do not know how sincere these applications are intended to be. It has been suggested in my home city of Saint John, and I am sure the thought has arisen elsewhere, that these may be applications put forward merely in the hope that an 80 per cent subsidy will be made available for allocation by the Transport Commission, as was mentioned last night by the hon. member for Crowfoot. On the other hand, I should like to know whether the two major railways seriously intend to do away with passenger service.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The last time such an application was made extensive hearings were held, and I thought it was then understood that within the foreseeable future, say 10 to 20 years, there would be no further applications made for passenger service discontinuance. The present proposal threatens a port city such as Saint John, dependent as it is on transportation. There is only one Canadian Pacific service to Saint John, from Montreal; the CN provides the other passenger link to Saint John from Moncton. Discontinuance of both these services is now being requested.
If the railways are serious about this, then it is a serious matter and something must be done about it. As I recall the recent legislation, provision is made for the Canadian Transport Commission to hold public hearings into such matters, and I for one make the request now that the transport commission be told to hold full hearings into the proposed application. I do not think this is a mandatory provision; nevertheless, I contend there should be full public hearings into the application to which I have referred in view of the serious economic cutbacks that would have to be made not only in Saint John but in the entire maritime region.
I am not simply talking about the abandonment of one extra railway fine, Mr. Speaker; I am referring to something that is the lifeblood of the entire maritime community, the two remaining railway links between Saint John and the outside world which are now threatened with abandonment.
Reference was also made last night to the previous hearings held by our transportation committee. Two or three years ago the committee travelled west to conduct extensive hearings into the need for the service offered by "The Dominion". On this committee were members who were very interested in transportation matters. The committee's enquiry
November 14, 1969
844	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada was also the forerunner of other committee studies. None of the recommendations made by this committee were pre-empted by the government, as has been the case with many other hearings recently. I give the government credit that they held back their decision until the committee were given a full opportunity to look into the future in the west of "The Dominion".
After considerable study the committee made some recommendations, one of which was that the service be continued. I think one of the reasons was that Expo '67 was approaching, but in any event the committee did not take a hard line. Although the CNR and CPR were offering another service in the area, the committee felt there was still a need for a transportation connection between various communities, though a full transcontinental connection of this nature was not required.
To a certain extent the railways took note of our recommendations. Railway representatives appeared before the committee and made a good impression. As we now begin to consider this new application during the next few months, I hope an opportunity will be given to the transportation committee to investigate fully, and that the government will not "jump the gun" by announcing its decision prematurely.
The Canadian Transport Commission also has a responsibility in such matters, though I am not quite sure where they fit into the picture. We all know the connection the present chairman of the transport commission has with this government. I do not know whether there is contact between the two, and I am not saying that there should not be; but I think practically everyone in Canada knows that the present chairman of the commission has been a supporter of the government for a long while.
I would think that the commission has some responsibility with regard to future policy. This morning I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about the recent increase in trucking rates in Ontario and Quebec. As I understand it, the truckers rate association has just approved increases that might total as much as 10 per cent in both provinces, and application is going to be made to the respective provincial boards for authority to make these increases. I should like to know where the Canadian Transport Commission fits in, and what action this government is taking. Is the


government approaching the transport commission on this matter? In view of the inflationary nature of these increases I would think the board certainly has some responsibility in this connection.
Legislation was recently passed in the maritimes to give trucking companies some of the benefits conferred upon the railways under maritimes rates legislation. It was thought that the truckers would then be able to compete with the railways, and that the maritimes would be better off as a result. This seemed to make sense. But if the news I heard this morning is correct, it means that the maritimes will now be faced with a further increase in trucking costs. It seems the minute we give the truckers authority to compete with the railways, they apply for increases in their own rates. When is the price spiral going to end? This sort of thing does not make sense to me.
Although the Canadian Pacific Railway is going to apply for discontinuance of the only passenger service from Montreal to Saint John, it is ironic that at this very moment a new passenger station costing $500,000 is under construction in Saint John. When questioned about this the CPR officials were straightforward, and I give them credit for that. They said they did not know whether discontinuance would be granted, so they had to go ahead and build the new passenger terminal anyway. Perhaps they are really hoping for a subsidy if they continue to provide service, and they will then use this new passenger terminal.
I have been unable to determine exactly where the responsibilities of the CPR begin and end. I do not complain about the CPR as much as I used to because they are making a $20 million investment for the Bay of Fundy at the moment. Nevertheless, I should like to know whether a subsidy is going to be paid, for which provision is made, I think, in the regulations of the transport commission.
As I have said, the Canadian Transport Commission must take its full responsibility in these applications and conduct public hearings. A study is presently being conducted in the maritimes, and there have been numerous studies of sundry transportation matters.
e (3:00 p.m.)
We have had dozens of studies covering all field of transportation. We had a study last year when the government wanted us to accept temporary legislation in this area. The Atlantic region transport study committee was set up to deal with all future problems of
November 14, 1969

transportation in the Atlantic region. We thought this was a good idea even though we knew it would result in a postponement of a solution to the major problem. That committee has had one meeting of not much importance. The members thought they should allocate selective assistance and they used many high-sounding words, some of which we have heard for a long time. In the meantime the increases have continued.
We had the surcharge increase in September, which has been mentioned in this House, and there is the possible increase in respect of Ontario and Quebec to which I referred a moment ago. We must face the fact that this increase may spread to the Maritimes. Still the studies continue. How do they all fit into the entire picture? I suggest very sincerely that we must know once and for all what the story is from the standpoint of Maritimes transportation.
We have been giving blanket approval each year of this type of legislation and have referred these matters to the appropriate committee. This is a desirable thing and there will be no effort on my part to hold up this legislation. The minister said it is similar to legislation passed in other years. I suppose that should satisfy us, but in view of the continuing increases and the indefiniteness of the transportation picture, particularly in the Maritimes, I take the opportunity to ask these questions with the hope that the minister will answer them.
We should have a statement in respect of the Air Canada picture and how it will be related to the many reports we have received. What are the possibilities of Air Canada becoming a privately-owned company? I am not talking about bond financing, as I realize that question has been dealt with, but what are the possibilities that Air Canada might become a privately-owned company with common stock available to the public?
I hope there will be an undertaking by the government about action to be taken in respect of increased transportation rates throughout the country. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to comment briefly on Bill C-7, authorizing the provision of moneys to meet the CNR's and Air Canada's deficits.
It may seem strange for a representative of a district which is not on the CNR line to take the floor this afternoon but first of all I want to say that I do so in the interest of the people of my constituency and in the light of the gigantic developments now under way there.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
This matter of transportation on the North Shore and of railroad connections has often been brought up in this House and in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
Not so long ago, the committee members paid a visit to my constituency. They were able to see the tremendous developments taking place in my riding, but were also quite disappointed with the lack of direct communication lines with other areas. There are a road and a number of harbors. We have access to the ocean through deep water ports, but we have no railway link with the rest of the continent.
I do not see why the CN, instead of thinking of abandoning some branch lines, should not try instead to improve, in certain areas, the quality of the service and especially to look into development opportunities in a riding such as mine.
When the committee visited the North Shore in September, the question of using ferryboats to travel between the North and the South Shores of the St. Lawrence was brought up.
In the small industrial town of Baie-Comeau, work is nearing completion on the construction of a fourth paper mill worth some $54 million. When this mill begins operations, production of newsprint will exceed
600,000	tons per year.
The management of this firm does not see why it should be necessary to look into


the possibility of establishing a ferry service between the South Shore and the North Shore so that this production may be brought to the large urban centres, to the American cities, by the regular CN railway lines.
On November 5, 1969, some representatives of the Quebec North Shore Paper Co. at Baie-Comeau handed me a brief entitled "Transportation needs on the North Shore of the Lower St. Lawrence". It reads as follows:
The availability of cheaper means of transportation is, today as in the past, an important factor of industrial development and expansion. Water transportation is now available year round in the Lower St. Lawrence region. But other and cheaper means of transportation-by water or by land-remain non-existent during the long winter months to move goods between localities on the North Shore and other points in Canada and North America.
This problem could be solved by establishing a train ferry service between Baie-Comeau and an economic railhead, and other points in Canada and North America.
In support of this proposal and on the assumption that composite shipments now carried on boats could be moved by rail, we respectfully ask you to consider the following facts.
In 1967, the shipping of composite shipments alone from Montreal and Quebec City to industrial communities on the North Shore amounted to 159,000 tons, which could be sent from Montreal and Quebec City by rail and then transferred to a train ferry as far as the North Shore. Bulk goods from Montreal and Quebec City to various points on the North Shore are generally forwarded by boat.
The combined volume of composite shipments from three ports on the North Shore to Quebec City and Montreal reached 14,000 tons in 1967. If to that westward traflc were added the 90,000 tons of newsprint which must now be shipped westward each year from Baie-Comeau through the St. Lawrence Seaway, it would create a balanced traflc of more than 100,000 composite cargo tons in both directions between localities on the North Shore and other western points.
We are presently studying the economic advantages of shipping our newsprint for places west of Baie-Comeau by rail-using train ferry operating all year round-in comparison with our present transportation system through the Seaway during the navigation season. Although the studies are not yet completed, we feel we should let you know the conclusions, since the possible establishment of a train ferry service would undoubtedly help you in your assessment of the transportation needs in the whole lower St. Lawrence area.
More than twenty years ago, one could still accept that the North Shore of the St. Lawrence had been forgotten in the construction of a system connecting the main centres essential to the development of Canada. Over the last two decades, however, the North Shore has become one of the regions of Canada which, per capita, contribute the most to the gross national product and this why it is no longer possible to ignore our area. In fact,
November 14, 1989

the North Shore is an "island" without any rail connection east of the Saguenay River. This "insularity" is still emphasized by the St. Lawrence River which prevents the establishment of any rail connection with South Shore railways.
Considering that during the winter months, Canadian and North American markets remain inaccessible to the North Shore by more economical means of transportation, we suggest that the committee might consider the possibility of including the North Shore among the "select territories" under the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act (17-18 Elizabeth II Chap. 52).
That is what was said in a brief I received recently. I do not raise this question for the first time. I think that we should give some attention to the problem. Once again, CN authorities might consider the potential development on the North Shore. When reference is made to rail service and connections between the North and the South Shores, the CN system serving the Maritimes is also involved. Instead of abandoning services, as is so often said, I do not see why the CNR management could not consider the possibility of buying the railroad connecting Mont-Joli with Matane, a distance of 40 miles, and add it to its system. A ferry service could then be operated from Matane to Baie-Comeau for the shipment of newsprint produced in the mill at Baie-Comeau.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
It is only 28 miles from Matane to Baie-Comeau. A rail-boat could easily operate between the two cities and thus encourage considerable development in that region.
In 1964, here in the House, I raised the question and the newspapers suggested the establishment of a railway link between the South Shore and the North Shore, resorting almost to the same arguments as I have just used.
Yet, I do not know whether the studies were carried out further by the management of the Canadian National Railways; however, I am aware that on the other side of the river, that is in my constituency, on the North Shore, very serious profitability studies have been made in that respect by private companies on behalf of the Canadian National Railways.
When the Committee on Transport and Communications went to the North Shore to study transportation problems there, a Canadian National Railway representative appeared before us in almost all the towns visited by the committee. I do not know what has been done since then, but I know that
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada some interest has been shown about the subject.
I should like to take this opportunity to deal with this problem because I know it will be referred to the Committee on Transport and Communications. We should look into it. As a matter of fact, the rail transport problem has become so serious in our area that the briefs, studies and requests addressed to the government should be taken into consideration.
A few days ago, not far from my riding, in Labrador City to be more precise, a disastrous airplane crash took eight lives. It was not possible to reach the scene for two days, because flying was the only way to get there. They finally had to use the Quebec North Shore Labrador Railway, a private railway, to reach the scene of the accident.
I deplore such facts and I would like to say that a population of 128,000 and a region developing at a fantastic pace, bringing an extraordinary contribution at the national level, must not be left without permanent railway lines. This responsibility is the government's own.
This is a rather reasonable attitude from the CNR authorities who are at least prepared to consider the rail-boat system which could be established as a link between the South Shore and the North Shore and which could, as studies and reports have shown, be profitable.
I wanted to make these comments and I hope that, when this bill is submitted to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, it can be studied as a whole and more information can be obtained.
If CNR officers hear my plea, I hope they will make the effort of examining briefs already submitted and that they will try and do something to have both sides of the river connected by rail.
