speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not take too much of the time of the House in voicing my opinion on Bill C-7 entitled:
An Act to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways System and Air Canada for the period from the 1st day of January, 1969, to the 30th day of June, 1970, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it should be noted that this bill is a replica of a similar bill introduced in
November 14, 1989
848	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada the fall of 1968 for the purpose of assisting the Canadian National Railways.
Now this morning, my colleague from Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) pointed out that last year, the Canadian National Railways made profits of $40 million, which were converted into deficits due to the payment of interest charges of $70 million, thus showing a deficit of some $30 million. If we compute the amount paid in interests in the last 25 years, we get the astronomical figure of $1,200 million paid in interest only on the C.N.R. debt.
From the way that Crown Corporation is administered, and at the rate finance is used in this particular case, it is clear that in about 10 years hence, the Canadian National Railways will ask us to authorize the abandon of all its lines throughout Canada.
The C.P.R. is asking to abandon its Mont-real-Toronto-Vancouver service, and now the C.N.R. is preparing to ask for permission to abandon its service to Lake St. John and from Abitibi to Montreal.
As for our region of Abitibi, it was born directly from the construction of what was then called the transcontinental railway.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
People left the areas north of Quebec or Montreal, to come and settle in Abitibi, along the railroad that was being built through Barraute, Senneterre, Amos, La Reine, La Sarre and Cochrane. It was the only railway from Montreal to western Canada which was an important area then. Cities like Toronto were less important in 1912, in 1913, at the time when the C.N.R., the transcontinental railway, was being built.
Today, we are asked to abandon that line, under the pretext that last year there was a deficit of $2 million in the operation of passenger trains between Abitibi and Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, no one talks, however, of the profits accrued to the Canadian National Railways through the transportation of freight and wood.
If the passenger service is abandoned in that area, how will we transport our lumberjacks, for instance, who come from Kamou-raska, Quebec, Cochrane, Hearst, and take them to Clova, Parent, Paradis, Bic, Senneterre, where there are still huge lumber operations.
Mr. Speaker, if the lumberjacks are unable to get to the operations, it will be pointless to continue the freight service since there will no longer be any wood to transport.


This morning, the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Lessard) spoke of the poor service given by the C.N.R. in his area, in our area, and he certainly was right. However, I was led to think, some seven or eight years ago, that if we had such bad service at home, if the prices were so frightfully high, if people did not care a bit for Abitibi or for Lac-Saint-Jean, it was because there were too many creditiste members in that area, and because we were not on the right side of the fence. I can recall the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean who was then a good Creditiste member, sitting on this side, with us; today, however he has turned Liberal.
In the Lac-Saint-Jean-Saguenay area, there are three Liberal members out of four, and instead of improving, services are deteriorating day after day, so that consideration is now being given to simply abandonning the line. It is worse than poor service: it is a total lack of it. However, the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean was right this morning, when he referred to the poor service provided on the Abitibi and Saguenay lines. Service between Lac-Saint-Jean and Quebec is so slow that it takes 12 hours to cover the distance. As for us, it takes us 17 hours because the distance is longer still.
Some lines have practically never been adjusted to the present needs allegedly, because it was too expensive. On the other hand, on the southern lines of the province and on some other lines there have been some improvements. Nothing is done for us. Quite recently, the passenger service between Rouyn-Noranda and Taschereau was abandoned, allegedly because it was unprofitable. Workers who had been with the C.N.R. 25 to 30 years were laid off; they were told the service had become uneconomic. And now it is going to be the turn of the Montreal-Abitibi-Rouyn-Noranda-Montreal-Lac - Saint-Jean-Saguenay line.
As for the cars, used in those areas, they are outdated equipment discarded by the Toronto-Montreal lines. Quite often, they use what we commonly call cattle cars in our area.
In days gone by, they used those cars for carrying oxen or cattle from the southern part of the province. We were given an old car, with separate seats, that was used 25 years ago in Montreal. Seats were repaired somehow or other. They finally got rid, about two years ago, of the little coal stove that was in a corner of the car.
November 14, 1969	COMMONS
That was the consideration given to our area. No wonder people do not travel by train any more. As for us, members of parliament, when we have to travel, we think it over twice before taking the train, because it is a 17-hour journey to Montreal.
We have to pay $22 now for a double bed. One can get accommodations at the Queen Elizabeth in Montreal for $18, and it is much more comfortable than the C.N.R. beds, especially in our area. It does not shake quite as much in the Queen Elizabeth unless you want it.
But aboard the train there is nothing you can do about it.
So I agree with what the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean said this morning and I hope that it is more than talk on his part.
A decision have to be made at one time or another as regards the Canadian National Railways. For instance, we must stand with all our might against the abandonment of those branch lines and, as I said a while ago, the C.N.R. was not established in order to make profits but to provide services. That was the reason for creating the Canadian National Railways, a public corporation.
We need those services in our area. As for the freight service, as I said earlier, the C.N.R. is making profits in our areas, but because they lose money in the passenger service, they think they should eliminate those lines. Is that the right thing to do? I ask the question. Some C.N.R. officials will read what I have just said.
What will happen to the lumberjacks who settled in that area? Are we going to transport them by helicopter as was the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during the last election campaign or will we find another means of transportation? Shall we transport them on the old wooden roads, in horse-drawn carriages because the motor car cannot be used? What shall we do with the lumberjacks since there are thousands of them in that area?
If there are no lumberjacks, the C.N.R. will have no wood to carry. This means that by suppressing at once the passenger service the day will come when they will suppress the freight cars and then the wood will not be moved to the large centres, such as Toronto, Montreal or Quebec.

speechtext:
There will be no newsprint either. At home we have all that. We are a

Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada little short on paper mills. We are not as spoiled as the Saguenay riding. In fact, the Saguenay area has a lot of paper to be moved. I thought earlier that the hon. member would ask for a railway line just above the St. Lawrence river, about 30 miles long, a floating highway, so that the C.N.R. could engage in transport operations there. However, one problem remains and I endorse his request to the effect that ferries should be used in order to equip these areas with means of transportation necessary to the development of their economy.
This is what I had to say with regard to the bill which deals once more, as always, with the financing of the deficits caused by interests paid to financiers and not by losses incurred in our areas.
If we could manage to establish a railroad between the financiers and the C.N.R. by eliminating taxes and interests, I think that there would be no more problems for the Canadian National Railways. There would be no more problems with Air Canada either.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The government is borrowing funds and then lending them to the C.N.R. As my colleague from Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) said it so well this morning they borrow at a rate of interest of 8-J, 8J or 8|- per cent, and they lend to the CN at a rate of 4j or 4 per cent.
Then, the government is surprised that the CN is faced with financial difficulties. The CN is not the only one to have difficulties. The government has some also and has no solution whatsoever. Even if the Prime Minister says that we are repeating ourselves, we are not any more than the system under which we rub along, because for at least 15 years, we have been passing the same act every year asking parliament to appropriate funds in order to help the "poor" CN.
If we had a sound financial system, not a stupid one, but a sensible one. But no. We are told: you keep saying that the monetary question will solve everything. But what is wrong, if not the financial system? That is what is wrong.
Our operations yield a $40 million profit, but the interest swallows up $70 million, so there is a deficit of $30 million. Let us pass Bill C-7 to make up this deficit and safeguard financial interests. The people who need railway service can always walk. Such is the present system: it moves backwards instead of progressing and creating something positive, because the financial problem will always hold us back.
November 14, 196S
850	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada
The minister can only say: Let us help the C.N.R. and Air Canada which are essential services. Yes, but at the same time let us stop financing those services through such ineffective and backward methods as those now used by the government.
This is our suggestion. The hon. member for Abitibi was quite right this morning; he quoted very accurate figures. Let us not forget that in 25 years from now, we will have to pay $1,200 million in interest only on the debt and no portion of the capital has been paid off. This reminds me of the notorious case of the Jacques Cartier bridge in Montreal, which cost $18 million, of which we have to date paid $21 million, in interest alone, and on which we still owe $14 million. When will the Jacques Cartier bridge be fully paid? If God does not know, our financial system can tell us!
As far as the railways are concerned, it is the same thing. The debt is never paid off, we cannot pay anything on it because our financial situation is bad. Inquiries of the president of the CN or of the president of Air Canada bring the answer that they cannot afford it, that they have no money. So, each year, a bill is introduced in the House and the members are told: Come to our help, we find ourselves in a dilemma, we are in debt, we must make up the deficit resulting from the interest on our debt! So, pass this bill, they tell us, in order that high finance may be protected and that the Canadian people be required to pay more taxes. That is exactly what it all comes to.
So, Mr. Speaker, we insist that the CN and Air Canada should be able to meet their obligations. But we hope that, at a given time, the government will come up with concrete proposals based on the system of monetary creation instead of superficial solutions based on the tax yield.
Let us go a little beyond this unscalable wall of human understanding which cannot see beyond taxation. The monetary system existed before taxes. Nowadays all our economic structure, including the structures of the CN and of Air Canada, is based on taxation instead of going to the root of matters and of relying on the creation scheme.
Then we say: Let us revert to the principle of creation. Why should we not call the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Louis Ras-minsky, who is an expert on financial questions, before the committee on transport and communications? We could ask him if, with the permission of the Canadian government


and all members, he would not advance the necessary funds to make up the deficit of Air Canada.
Then, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, will reply: If parliament tells me to do so, I certainly will.
Preventing the chartered banks from multiplying that creation fourteenfold would solve the problem. The losses of the CN and Air Canada would be paid off. Let us stop paying interest on a nominal debt. Let us start by becoming the masters of our own financial system; then we can say that our national undertakings, our Crown corporations belong to the Canadian people and not to those who stole from them by exacting interests of $1,200 million in the last 25 years.
Mr. Speaker, the minister who is listening to me is not mentally retarded; he is an intelligent man. He knows full well what I mean. He knows that I am right, but he cannot say so. He knows also that if the sovereign parliament asks the Governor of the Bank of Canada to create the necessary credits, the Governor will say that he is entitled to do so. If parliament instructs him to do so, he can do it. However, no one dares ask him. Mr. Rasminsky is allowed to welcome, in his office, the top representatives of the big financial institutions, of the chartered banks; transactions, plots, follow, to maintain the financial system which is making slaves of us.
Mr. Speaker, these are the few observations I wanted to make on the gaps created by a stupid system and on the means of correcting them, that is, by levying additional taxes. That is what it will come to: The Canadian people will have to pay more taxes to make up deficits.
Mr. Speaker, we do not object to everything. Far from it. We are opposed however to the CNR ceasing to provide service in the North, to the Lake St. John and Saguenay region. I ask that the CNR increase its services to attract customers, that its trains move a little faster and bring people from Rouyn, Amos, La Sarre or Chicoutimi to Montreal. In fact it should provide good service and make available to the public comfortable cars, attractive ones, with even television aboard as on planes nowadays. It should pay attention to the people. If the passenger service is good it might become more profitable and it could thus be possible to keep on assuring transportation to workers and lumbermen in a still very important region with regard to lumber operations. The CNR will continue to do business as long as
November 14, 1969

these services are attractive and run for the benefit of the population.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no subject will arouse in a Maritimes Member of Parliament more passion or justifiable outrage than the subject of transportation. Not 102 years ago but two years ago, on the 100th anniversary of the founding of this nation, we witnessed an event that sounded the death-knell for many industries in the Atlantic region. Notwithstanding all its talk about the just society and the elimination of regional disparities, this government did nothing to rectify what took place in the Atlantic region. Almost every month the Atlantic community hears more bad news about transportation. It is difficult, indeed almost impossible, for me to suggest how much longer the economy of our area can withstand the repercussions of freight rate increases, railway lay-offs and the elimination of services which industry in the Atlantic region needs in order to survive.
In August, 1967, the railways were given the right to increase non-carload tariffs within the Atlantic region. The increases took effect in September of that year and we objected to them as strongly as we could. Every area of the community lodged its objection with the government, but it was all without avail and the increases took effect. As a result, many businesses and jobs have been eliminated in the Atlantic provinces.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
In time-and it took a lot of time-the government amended the Maritime Freight Rates Act to allow trucking firms in the Atlantic area certain subsidies which up until that time had been available only to the railways. This step was of major assistance to industry in the area because for the first time it was not a captive customer of the railways. I have not noticed any significant reduction in freight rates as a result of the extension of subsidies to the trucking industry. In fact, I do not believe that industry in our area is receiving the full benefit of the extension of these freight subsidies. Shippers in the Atlantic provinces should make their justifiable grievances known so that they receive a full measure of benefit from the extension of the freight rates subsidies. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) should watch closely
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada what the trucking industry does with regard to freight rates in the region as a result of the extension of subsidies.
The shippers of the region should know there are teeth in the legislation which was passed, and that the trucking industry has a right to react in a favourable manner to those shippers. After all, the objective of the extension of the subsidies was to create a system of freight rates which would be more helpful for the survival of industry in the area. Soon after the government undertook to extend the freight rate subsidies to the trucking industry, it allowed the railways to remove the freeze on carload lot shipments. As a result, a still greater burden was placed on shippers in the Atlantic region. Recently, Canadian National Railways decided to take a further step. Without consultation with the Minister of Transport, I understand they decided to eliminate all less than carload lot traffic coming into the Atlantic region from the rest of Canada. When I learned of this action, I immediately contacted the Minister of Transport. The minister was quick to take action and as a result these freight rate changes were not allowed to take effect and the CNR was forced to continue providing an l.c.l. service to the Atlantic region. It would have been an additional blow to the industry in the region if the shippers who depend upon l.c.l. traffic to bring supplies in with which to manufacture goods, which often have to be shipped out of the region, had been forced to pay higher express rates. This would have happened had the CNR been allowed to continue with its objective of putting the new rates into effect on November 3 of this year.
I believe the Minister of Transport endeavours to do his best to protect the region. It is not his fault that we are without a transportation policy which would give protection and hope for the future of industry in the area. I think he is doing his best, but the cabinet is doing little to assist him. While all this is going on, employees of the railways in the region are suffering one cutback after another. We are told this is for the sake of efficiency. It is a shocking way to achieve efficiency. After	25 years of service,
employees are suddenly finding themselves unemployed.
I have before me a communication which I received from Mr. Carl H. Hiltz, the educational chairman of local No. 9 of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers. He informed me that men with as long as 30 years' service were
852	COMMONS
Private Members' Public Bills released from their employment without more than two weeks' notice. I wrote the vicepresident of the Atlantic region regarding this matter. He accepted the fact there may be problems in relation to the unemployment being created by the railway for the sake of efficiency and stated he would look into the matter. At the same time he informed me that the Atlantic region express operations of the CNR would be reduced from 50 locations to 17 or 18. That is more very bad news for the employees of that region.
This is just the beginning, Mr. Speaker, of the issues I wish to bring to the attention of the House with regard to this bill. I would now like to call it four o'clock.

subsubtopic: PROVISION TO ASSURE PUBLIC RIGHT OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS AND INFORMATION
speechtext:
that Bill C-20, to better assure the public's rights to freedom of access to public documents and information about government administration, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in support of Bill C-20, an act to better assure the public's right to freedom of access to public documents and information about government administration, it seems that I could hardly do so at a more timely juncture. It is
[Mr. Coates.)
DEBATES	November 14, 1969
just over a year ago that the same bill was talked out in this chamber by government members. At that time one or two government members, when adding their voices to the debate, pointed out that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was no doubt concerned about participatory democrary and in his enthusiasm for a well-informed public had set up a task force on government information.
a (4:00 p.m.)
As we all know, Mr. Speaker, the task force has reported and its report, from pages 25 to 34, contain a detailed examination and criticism of the hush-hush secrecy now observed by the government together with some excellent comparisons between Canada's outmoded procedures in this area and those of other countries, notably Sweden. So my hopes soar high today that hon. members opposite will be heartened by these events, and disposed to allow this bill to go to an appropriate committee where it may be treated as raw material useful in helping to bring Canada up-to-date by opening the windows and unbarring the doors of official reticence.
As the bill states in its explanatory note, it is being presented in aid of the public right to know in what manner the government is administering the public duties entrusted to it by the people. The key clause states:
Every administrative or ministerial commission, power and authority shall make its records and information concerning its doings available to any person at his request in reasonable manner and time.
The measure provides for certain specific exemptions to this provision where these would be in the public interest. In brief, it puts into words-words which I hope will become law-the basic parliamentary, democratic principle that public affairs must be conducted publicly. Is it not incongruous that though, according to the task force on government information, close to $150 million is expended annually on circulating the type of information which the government wants to put out, many motions placed on the order paper of this House by private members call in vain for the production of the type of information which the public wants and which apparently the government denies? My hon. friend the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) stated recently:
It is ironic that the Prime Minister co-authored a manifesto in 1964 entitled an Appeal for Realism in Politics which said that democratic progress requires the ready availability of true and complete information".
November 14, 1969

Further, I would remind the House that within the last two months the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) himself stated:
Government secrecy is sometimes legitimized as the state's right to privacy but it may well be a denial of the public right to know.
A great deal has been published on this general subject by the press of Canada. To quote but one opinion, the Toronto Globe and Mail in an editorial entitled "It is the public's business" had this to say:
One bad side effect of the prodigious growth of government in this century is that it has become exceedingly difficult to keep track of. Not only are governments themselves much more deeply and widely involved in the life of the people, but their tasks have become so numerous that they have had to delegate much of their authority to boards and commissions. Accompanying this governmental growth has been a disinclination on the part of governments and their creatures to keep the public informed about what they are doing.
A private bill has been presented to the House of Commons which could do much to open these many closed doors and keep the public informed about what is, after all, its own business. The bill would require that "every administrative or ministerial commission, power and authority shall make its records and information available to any person at his request in reasonable manner and time".
Exceptions would be made for matters of national security, matters exempted by statute from disclosure, trade secrets, commercial information obtained from private persons and subjects of private interest "to the degree that the right to personal privacy excludes the public interest".
It is my idea, Mr. Speaker, that if this bill becomes law the enforcing agency should be the Exchequer Court of Canada. In urging that the House allow the subject matter of the bill to go to a committee, I feel this is in line with the expressed sentiments of government leaders, as well as with the findings of the task force on government information, and that what it proposes could be a potent ingredient of improved parliamentary democracy in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to listen to the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather). He frequently introduces a philosophical note into our debates in this House, and if I might be permitted to be personal about an hon. member for a moment, he possesses another characteristic, that of a great tenacity. He has chosen certain areas of special concern, for example, the field of auto safety and items such as the one he has brought before us today. I have had the pleasure of serving on committees at which he was present and I know of his concern about the effects of smoking on health. It seems logical
Private Members' Public Bills that today he should introduce Bill C-20 to better assure the public's rights to freedom of access to public documents and information about government administration.
As the hon. member has told us, this bill is concerned with opening windows and unbarring doors. It is based on the idea that public affairs must be conducted publicly, to use the words which are to be found in the explanatory notes of the measure we are considering. I am forced immediately to consider what would be the results for the government, for the House of Commons, and indeed for the citizens of this country, if we were to follow generally such practices as are now followed when the government presents documents called, somewhat oddly it appears to me, white papers. In recent weeks two important white papers have been published, one on veterans affairs and another on taxation. These documents, both of which are likely to become famous if they are not so already, represent attempts by the government to carry on its business in the open. It seems to me that they are genuine attempts-indeed, the attempt has become an accomplished fact

to place before the people of the country the issues as the government sees them and then to wait for response and reaction.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This morning I happened to listen to a radio program on this very subject, and I want to refer to it briefly. The program is entitled "Dialogue", and on the program this morning there were two individuals well known to the Canadian public, especially those who listen to the media, Pierre Berton and Charles Templeton. They were discussing not so much the white paper on taxation but what this bill is all about, namely whether or not a government ought to carry on its business openly before the public.
They were using the white paper on taxation as a kick-off for the discussion, and an interesting thesis was put forward, one that sort of surprised me at first, as I am sure it will surprise many hon. members of this House. This thesis was that government should not be guided by the public's reaction to its statements of intention.
I must interject that Bill C-20 does not say that all the business of government should be made known to the public, but that most things should, with some exceptions listed in the bill.
When the business of government is done before the public, it was the contention of
November 14, 1969

Private Members' Public Bills these two gentlemen that it is those who are wealthy and powerful who raise the loudest protests and are best able to finance and mount campaigns against a certain aspect of a government program or other programs that will work to their own detriment or to the detriment of their vested interests. In other words, by virtue of the fact that government makes a statement of intention or opens its books to the public, it is giving the wealthy an advantage over the poor.
These two gentlemen also suggested that if government should happen to listen to the response that it gets-and there was a real argument that it ought not listen to the response it gets for the reason I have just put forward-it will always receive an impression that is heavily weighted in favour of the strong, in favour of the established and the wealthy. Equally this results in creating an impression that is to the disfavour of the voiceless poor, those who are disestablished in society at any given point in time but constitute a very important segment of society, one that ought to be getting priority from government if total social justice is to be done.
This point seems to me to be exactly on the subject that is before the House for debate this afternoon. I would have to draw some conclusions about this question, and my conclusions are as follows: First, it would seem to me that government should make its actions and its statements of intention public. It would seem to me that the policy that is being carried out by the present government of issuing white papers, for example, is a very good one. Second, the response of the public to such statements of intention must always be treated with a healthy degree of skepticism. Third, it would seem to me that good government does not simply depend on open government; rather, it depends on responsible actions on the part of those who are entrusted to do the nation's business in the people's name.
As I suggested at the outset, this bill raises, for me at least two very basic philosophical and psychological questions. The first is: Is it true that all power corrupts? And to finish that off: Is it true that absolute power corrupts absolutely?

Well, we will not have to test that. If it is the case that all power does tend to corrupt, then it is incumbent upon people in positions of authority, if there is to be any sort of justice done, that there be some kind


of built-in system of checks and balances; that there be a system in our nation-since we are talking about the government of the country-whereby the persons in whose hands power lies can be called to account for their administration and their action.
Surely we who make up government in Canada are called to account. No one can go through an election campaign and not be intimately, bitterly, personally and joyfully aware of how we are called to account. On the same point of power corrupting, and so on, may I elaborate further and point out that we live in a society where people pride themselves very much on being open-minded. Similarly, this bill suggests that we ought to have open government for open-minded people. There is a kind of "put down" for people who keep pushing the open-minded idea which goes as follows, that you can be so open-minded that all your brains fall out. The point here is that to tolerate everything and to object to nothing is a good pushed to its logical extreme. If you push a good to its logical extreme, it comes out as an evil.
Similarly, as far as Bill C-20 is concerned, although open government is a good thing, I submit that it is possible to be so "open-governed" that action on any issue could become almost impossible. Some segments of society would be displeased by it. If this idea were enshrined in law, it would be possible to be so open-governed that all the power would fall out of government. Government stripped of the power to govern must surely be a contradiction in terms.
This bill also underscores something near and dear to the hearts of all those who deal with people. It seems to me that no one has more to do with all varieties of human nature than the politician, those of us who represent the people of Canada in this House.
The big cry today-it is also the underlying idea in this bill-is that we should all be for participatory democracy. Participatory democracy has become a kind of sacred cow and no one "knocks" or questions it. However, I wonder whether it ought not to be held up to a little ridicule once in a while. It seems to me that participatory democracy is based on the assumption that everybody ought to have a share in running everything all the time. It is very fortunate-or unfortunate, depending on your point of view-that most people have neither the time nor the competence to run everything all the time. Therefore, if one is to be realistic, as long as human nature is human nature and societies
November 14, 1969	COMMONS
are societies, power will inevitably tend gradually to migrate into the hands of a few.
This small group into whose hands the power to govern passes consists of those who are believed to be the most capable and meritorious by their benefactors and supporters; or, on the other side of the coin, those who are considered to be the shrewdest charlatans by their detractors and opponents. So it depends what side of the fence you are on whether you think those into whose hands the power has fallen are the worst people in the world or the best. Let me read a quotation from John Stuart Mill. I want to read this into the record because I think it has a direct bearing on the bill before us. He said:
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
We owe our capacity to bear with the passing errors of society to man's faculty of rectifying his own mistakes, not by experience alone. There must be discussion to show how experience is to be interpreted.
By way of interjection here let me say that that surely would be a useful definition of what Parliament or the House of Commons is all about.
Mill goes on to say:
The whole strength and value of human judgment depends upon one property, that it can be set right when it is wrong, reliance can be placed upon it only when the means to set it right are kept constantly at hand.
I would draw the attention of the chamber this afternoon to the final words, "only when the means to set it right are kept constantly at hand." Surely, some of the means which are available to us in Canada to set things right are the ballot-boxes and the education of our citizens. Surely, we also agree that to educate the people of Canada, for example to make my constituents or the constituents of any other member of this House fully aware of the intricacies of the issues before Parliament at any time, would be and is a full-time job. If I were to do a proper job of educating my constituents about what is going on here I would not have time to do anything else; indeed, I would not have time to appear here or carry on the work expected of a member.
Therefore, I am pleased that the report of the task force on government information states that governments themselves, indeed this government in particular, must spend more of its resources educating the people. In this sense I am sure the hon. member for Surrey is pleased with the task force report. Indeed, he made reference to it. Knowing the

One ought to be, in any event. We find that they are not always the same people who in this House deserve the impression that has been created in the mythology of this country. One is well aware that certain members work very hard and obviously do excellent work. However, through the news media, which is a kind of "bitch" goddess of our times, we never hear of them; they are never seen or complimented. Other members of Parliament who in some ways do far less seem always to be before the public. This in itself seems to be a powerful argument for conveying more and better information to the citizens of Canada. It is important that our people should be better informed. Simply giving access to the documents of government, as Bill C-20 suggests, will not do this. We need to adopt some of the recommendations contained in the report of the task force. I should like to read one section and its principal recommendation, which appears in volume 1 at page 61. The recommendation is as follows:
We recommend that:
1. The right of Canadians to full, objective and timely information and the obligation of the state to provide such information about its programs and policies be publicly declared and stand as the foundation for the development of new government policies in this field. This right and obligation might be comprehended within a new constitution in the context of freedom of expression.
I agree with this entirely. However, at the moment, lacking full and efficient means of spreading government information-you can call it propaganda if you will, or information as to what government is all about-we are thrown to the mercies of the news media as it now exists. Let me conclude by giving one
856	COMMONS
Private Members' Public Bills illustration which demonstrates to me at least that we are in very fickle hands. The government's white paper on taxation came out just a week ago. Headlines in some papers said essentially, "Higher taxes" and then in fine print, "for the well to do". One might just as well say, "lower taxes for those on lower incomes". Which is right? The truth is that both are right. I hesitate to name newspapers so I shall not do so, but the two newspapers which I read followed this pattern. One essentially ran a headline which could be summarized in two words, "Tax increases". Thousands of readers of that paper are not in government and do not really know what is going on.

As reported at page 550 of Hansard, my distinguished colleague the hon. member for Saint John-Lan-caster (Mr. Bell) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) this question:
Mr. Speaker, have the Prime Minister and his colleagues taken note of the recommendations of the task force on government information which state there is a specific need for the government to provide more informative replies to questions raised in Parliament than has been the tradition and, if so, what does he plan to do about it?
Of course, we found the usual movement toward secrecy on the part of the Prime Minister, who wiggled and evaded the question. The hon. member used the word "educate" or "lead". The hon. member who introduced the bill spoke about the state having a right to privacy. The state has no right to privacy. It is in no better nor worse position than the people who place the government in power and give it a limited opportunity to govern. Any taxpayer is entitled to say to the government, "This is my money that you are spending to secure this information. Why should you hide it from me?" I recognize there are exceptions. The hon. member has placed some of these exceptions in the second clause of his bill. I could think of others, but think particularly of the exemption provided under subparagraph (b) concerning matters that are exempted by statute from disclosure.
If this government, which has the onus of justifying to Parliament that there are special reasons, can say there are special reasons- and places those reasons before us-why matters to which it may become privy should not be made public, I am sure the exception would be granted by Parliament. But I believe the fundamental rule is that the state has no inherent right to privacy. I take that position with all the strength at my command. Unfortunately, many governments are moving not in the direction of a greater degree of openness but more in the direction of secrecy.
I had the honour to be a member of a committee which on the last day of the last session filed a report dealing with statutory instruments. It was a remarkable experience to be a part of that committee. We listened to distinguished members of the civil service who appeared before us and gave evidence concerning the measure of secrecy which prevails in respect of the origin and actual promulgation of many orders in council and ministerial decrees which affect to a large extent the lives and fortunes of very many citizens of this country. I was amazed, as I think anyone would be who read the record, at the inherent and implied criticism of the processes of government which were laid open as a result of the deliberations and the report of that committee.
Finally, as a member of the bar who has spent a great many years engaged in the art of advocacy, while there are many ways in which the administration of justice and the practice before the courts could be improved I wonder just how far we would have gone in
Private Members' Public Bills the settlement of disputes between citizen and citizen or between citizen and the state if the old practices of the Star Chamber at the time of Strafford and Laud were still in effect. There is a rule that unless one of the parties to a trial is able to convince the court that a matter should be held in camera, all judicial proceedings are open. The participants, the accused person if it should be a criminal trial, and the witnesses are exposed to the full light of publicity before their fellow citizens in the community. The evidence is given under oath in the pitiless glare of publicity in open court. If that practice did not prevail, Mr. Speaker, the cases of injustice perpetrated on the people of our country would be magnified greatly.
It is because justice is open that justice generally is good. There is great room for improvement and I believe we are moving in this direction, but if that provision of openness, which I think is the fundamental one were not present, I wonder where we would be in respect of the administration of justice in this or any country.
I have one final point which concerns our good friends who look down upon us and tell the public what happens in this chamber. One reason they are not here in great numbers when they should be, particularly to hear this debate, is that they are compelled to wander from building to building and from minister to minister seeking scraps of information. If everything were made public as it should be, the members of the press gallery would be here and our proceedings would be more widely and elaborately reported. That is one reason I am glad, on behalf of gentlemen of the press gallery, to support this bill. I am sure from the smiles opposite that the government will support the bill, that it will receive second reading and go on to be duly dealt with in the other place.

First, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) who, incidentally, is a journalist and therefore brings to the subject matter of this bill a particular knowledge which I think merits considerable respect from all parts of the House.
I am sure it is no coincidence that this bill comes before us almost contemporaneously with the tabling of the recent task force report on government information entitled
858	COMMONS
Private Members' Public Bills "To Know and Be Known". I think that possibly this bill proffers some solutions and recommendations in an area where the report of the task force did a very find job of identifying and recognizing problems without coming forward with specific recommendations.
The subject matter of this bill covers an area of direct concern which is not perhaps the major item covered by the task force report but is one major item in it. I confess that I have not read the entire report of the task force because I found that in an effort to be "with it" and to be "now", the literary style of the task force report in effect made it rather tedious reading; before I had read many chapters I found it rather heavy going.
I think they have adopted a rather strange literary style so as to attract attention. While it may be rather effective for several paragraphs or even a couple of chapters, it tends to be boring as one goes through a book-length document. Not having completed it, I would not pretend to suggest that the same fault lies with the conclusions reached, but I certainly find it hard going and I am sure this was not what the drafters intended.
The task force report, in an area particularly relevant to this bill, pointed out that governments, like people, are very much subject to their heredity and their environment. Although we are living in a day where participatory democracy is a prominent phrase- hopefully, considerably more than a slogan and certainly something which many people and institutions in this country are attempting to achieve-we are also living with a tradition or an heredity of administrative secrecy which is not compatible with the concept of participatory democracy.
The report of the task force goes on to cite the United States experience. It points out that of necessity the congressional system has caused a breakdown of secrecy because in fact the administration must, in justifying its programs and conclusions to the legislative branch, disclose the processes by which it has arrived at those recommendations and conclusions. The democratic system and functions of government in the United States do not appear to have suffered tremendously from their ability to get along without this type of secrecy which we have inherited probably from the days of absolute monarchy.
We have probably also inherited this type of secrecy from the closed-family governing classes of Great Britain which were prominent in the early part of the last century.

DEBATES	November 14, 1969
Fortunately, I think my friends in the New Democratic Party can cite the Swedish tradition with considerably more validity so far as I am concerned, and I accept it as having more validity than many of the other parallels in Sweden which they cite. The right of access by the citizen to public information is a matter of constitutional right in Sweden and one which the government agency choosing to deny access to public documents can only exercise after having proved that the interest of the country is better served by not making the disclosure.
The task force report also reviews the experience in Great Britain on this matter. I think this,, again, is an experience parallel to the one which our task force presents to us; it is one where the problem is well identified and recognized but to which no solution is offered. Following the original report to the British government, a government white paper was filed in which, again, great difficulty was encountered when it came to finding practical solutions to this very real problem.
As I said before, the task force report offers no recommendations in this area. Perhaps, considered concurrently with the hon. member's bill, we may have the start of a substantial recommendation in the solution of this problem. I hope sincerely that together with the task force report this bill will receive second reading and be referred to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, it is an interesting coincidence, that this bill introduced by the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather) should come before the House just about two weeks after the task force on government information tabled its report.
Still, I believe that there are few distinctions to be made. The hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather)-and I congratulate him for his initiative and for his interest in this question-has introduced Bill C-20, an Act to better assure the Public's Rights to Freedom of Access to Public Documents and Information about Government Administration (Administrative Disclosure).
We read, in the explanatory note, and 1 quote:
This bill is in aid of the public's right to know ir. what manner a government is administering the public duties entrusted and delegated to it by the people: save for exceptions that are in the public interest, the bill enacts Bentham's basic parliamentary Rule that public affairs must be conducted publicly.
November 14, 1969

Private Members' Public Bills
I understand that the task force's report on government information services advocates an information policy
There is nothing concerning an information policy in the bill presented today by the hon. member for Surrey, but the bill deals with the rights to freedom of access to public documents and information. I do not quarrel with the rights to freedom of access to public documents and information, when need arises, for that was also pointed out in the task force's report.
I believe I can tell the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) what the government is going to do with the task force's report on information services.
And I think I am in a position to do it by quoting comments that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is reported as having made in 1964 when he was not yet a member of parliament.
In an article published in an issue of Cite Libre in 1964, under the title: "Pour une politique fonctionnelle", he stated:
Progress In democracy requires the availability of accurate and complete information so as to enable the people to assess government policies with full knowledge of the facts. Otherwise, obscurantist autocracy prevails. Yet in many sectors, it is very difficult, if not impossible, for citizens to make sound political judgments.
You will tell me that the Prime Minister is not alone in the cabinet! No, I agree, although he may give an impetus to the policy that he intends to pursue. But shortly before the report of the task force on information was published, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) told the Canadian Bar Association, about two months ago:
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)

If individual privacy is a foundation of democracy the citizen's right to know is fundamental to any participatory democracy.
The public cannot be expected to dialogue meaningfully-still less decide-if it is refused the very information which would make such a dialogue and decision-making possible.

Another member of the cabinet, the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans), stated not so long ago, and I quote:

I'm willing to publish any and all documents that show gaps in our organization except those which contain critical comments about specific people.

Another minister of this government, the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) said not so long ago, and I quote: [English]
I don't see why we shouldn't be able to quote public servants any less than we quote consultants. These people are professionals.

And the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry added:

You don't suppress something because you don't want it exposed to counter argument. This is lethal in the long-term. You don't suppress reports drawn up by competent people at the public expense.

I could go on quoting several other statements made by ministers of this government. This shows that this government had and still has the intention of promoting a policy on information. I am sure, in the light of what the ministers have already said, that the task force report will be used as a basis for the establishment of a policy on information.
I do not intend, Mr. Speaker, to give you a summary of the task force report, since the previous speakers did so, but it must be known that the right to information is not the sole prerogative of newspapermen. I am not saying that this is what the hon. member for Surrey had in mind. I am just expressing a personal opinion. The right to information does not only belong to newspapermen or mass media, but to the public at large.
What about the interpretation of information? This is a very important element. The general public receives its information through the large media which often colour it somehow. Can we then say that it is information? I do not think so.
Who will therefore decide which type of information should be available to the public? Should we divide citizens into categories? Should we give different information to the members of parliament and to the newspapermen? Should we give another type of information to other news, media, and still another type to the general public?
This report leads the way. It contains advice and proposals and I am sure these will be given serious consideration by the government when it tables legislation in this field.

Should Canada leave it to a minister of Information to decide what information should be given? Should such decisions be left to a minister, to a committee of ministers, or, as is done in Sweden, to administrative commissions quite distinct from the legislative power? The question is a vital one and I know that the hon. member of the New Democratic Party was right to raise it. Anyway, we are not prepared to make this decision specially since, as I am practically sure, most if not all members either have not read the whole report or have not assimilated it.
Therefore, I am not prepared to make a decision. Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock?
